prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in such moire structures

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first. It is the one candidate on this shortlist that every member ranked (eight of eight, the highest Borda total), and the breadth matters more to me than any single first place: members who start from very different fields still place it between rank 1 and rank 6. It is a concrete discovery in the sense I look for first. A quantitative prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) said that flat bands should appear at a specific angle, and seven years later the experiment (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018) found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. Prediction followed by confirmation, then a large reproduced literature across many moire platforms, is what I would want to see before honouring a field. The theory-plus-experiment trio is natural, and the physics is not an engineering refinement of something recognised before.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity of understanding rather than of observation. The facts are reproduced by many groups, but the pairing mechanism is unsettled, and five or six colleagues (Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson, Kroll) said this is early or young in interpretation. The credit is also not clean. Cao, the first author of the 2018 experiments, is outside any three-name configuration, other experimental groups made independent contributions, and earlier moire-band theory exists. If the committee wants a stable interpretation before awarding, topological insulators (B047) or optical lattice clocks (B010) are the safer, more mature choices.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a reorganisation of how phases are classified, with a topological invariant rather than a broken symmetry, and treats the case as if anything overdue; he also notes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D work are left out.
responses.response: I agree on the conceptual weight and ranked B047 second myself. Where I differ is that the attribution problem there looks harder to me than it does for twisted bilayer graphene. A three-name cap forces a choice among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan, with Bernevig, Hughes and the late Shoucheng Zhang excluded, and the 2016 prize on topological phases lowers the novelty. For twisted bilayer graphene the prediction and the discovery are one clean chain with a fairly natural trio. I accept his point that B047 is the more mature field, and I would not oppose it if the committee finds the attribution can be settled.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first for the improvement in what we can measure and how accurately, and sees the maturity as timely because the performance is confirmed in many laboratories and the redefinition of the second is pending.
responses.response: I left the clock candidate off my own opening ranking, and I should say why. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the list and the confirmation is excellent. My hesitation is that it is a refinement of a measurement capability whose underlying ideas (laser cooling, frequency combs, ion clocks) were largely recognised in 1997, 2005 and 2012. The case would be stronger if the committee can frame the novel physics (magic-wavelength trapping and the tests of relativistic redshift at millimetre scales) rather than the precision alone. I take his point seriously enough to list B010 as an alternative, but I do not think precision by itself outranks the opening of a new regime of matter.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene fourth, noting that it is conceptually clear and influential but somewhat early because the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, and that the junior first author is not credited.
responses.response: I take the 'somewhat early' point as the main risk to my own choice, and I do not dismiss it. My answer is that the prize would honour the platform and the observation of the correlated and superconducting phases, which do not depend on a settled pairing mechanism, much as earlier prizes honoured observed phenomena before their full explanation. On the first-author issue I agree that the three-person limit is a real injustice to Cao and I would want the citation to speak of the discovery of the states rather than imply the credit is exhaustive.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first, as an instrumental and scientific achievement that opened a new observational window, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene second.
responses.response: I put IceCube third and I share his view that neutrino astronomy is a real discovery of nature. Our difference is on maturity and credit. As he notes, the diffuse flux is confirmed mainly by one experiment, with KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD still catching up, and the source identifications are statistically modest. Credit inside a collaboration of hundreds is hard to narrow to Halzen, Karle and Spiering, and the roles of the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers are open. I think this becomes easier to defend in a few years. It is a serious alternative and the support of both of us for it is not trivial, but I would not prefer it to the graphene case today.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, and says the architecture underlies most superconducting quantum processors, while flagging the closeness of the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits and his own bias toward the area.
responses.response: I respect his declared bias and his candour about the 2025 overlap, and I agree it is the main difficulty for B041. I ranked it eighth for the same reason. A prize that shares a platform and a recent citation with last year's award will be read as an extension of that one, and the omission of Girvin and Huang from the three names makes the credit less clean. I would rather wait than give a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon.

uncertainties: Whether the citation should centre on the prediction, the experiment, or both, and how to reflect the omission of Cao and other experimental groups from a three-person cap.
Whether the unsettled superconducting pairing mechanism makes recognition now premature compared with the more mature topological insulators.

Whether the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is sufficiently distinguished from precursor moire-band theory (for example by Dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto and others) to credit the trio without objection.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My field is string theory, gravity and cosmology, far from moire materials, topological insulators or atomic clocks. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not involve any shortlisted candidate. I also lack condensed-matter expertise and rely partly on my recollection of priority.
